title: After vibe coding: 16 things to learn, in order
dek: Vibe coding gets you a demo. These 16 ideas are what it takes to build an AI product that works. Four levels, one video each.

blocks.html: You can make an app by talking to an AI now. That is vibe coding, and it is a good start. But the words in every AI job post and every engineering blog are different ones: tokens, RAG, MCP, evals.

Here are 16 of them, in the order they build on each other. Each level needs the one before it. Each term has one line on what it is and one video that explains it well. Where only part of a video is needed, the link starts there. Total: under 3 hours.

items.what: The pieces a model reads and writes. Not words: vibe coding is several of them. You pay per token and the context window is counted in them.
items.title: Most devs don't understand how LLM tokens work
items.why: Short and practical: what a token is, why you pay per token, and why some words and languages cost more.

items.what: Text turned into a list of numbers, so that things with similar meaning sit close together. Search and RAG are built on this.
items.title: Embeddings: What they are and why they matter
items.why: Simon Willison, who co-created Django and writes one of the most-read AI blogs, shows what embeddings do for a builder: related posts and search by meaning.

items.what: Find the right pages first, put them in the prompt, then let the model answer. How you give a model your own documents.
items.title: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?
items.why: Six minutes from an IBM Research scientist. One known date slip: the Saturn moon count in her example is out of date. The idea is not.

items.what: Make the model answer in an exact shape, like JSON with fixed fields, so your code can read it. Tool calling is built on this.
items.title: OpenAI DevDay 2024: Structured outputs for reliable applications
items.why: The engineers who built the feature explain why asking for JSON breaks, and how a schema fixes the shape. It fixes the shape, not whether the content is right.

items.what: The model does not run anything. It asks your code to run a function, with the arguments filled in, and reads the result.
items.title: LLM Function Calling - AI Tools Deep Dive
items.why: Shows the real round trip in code: tool definition, the model's request, your code running it, the result going back.

items.what: One standard plug between AI apps and tools. Write a tool once and every MCP app can use it.
items.title: Model Context Protocol Clearly Explained | MCP Beyond the Hype
items.why: Starts from the problem MCP solves, then opens a real server and shows its tools. Honest that it is early days.

items.what: A model in a loop: plan, call a tool, check the result, go again, until the job is done.
items.title: How We Build Effective Agents: Barry Zhang, Anthropic
items.why: From a co-author of Anthropic's “Building effective agents”: tools in a loop, and when not to build an agent at all.

items.what: What the agent keeps between steps and between chats, and how it gets it back when it needs it.
items.title: The Four Types of Memory Every AI Agent Needs
items.why: The four kinds of memory, each with an example a builder already uses, like a CLAUDE.md file.

items.what: Deciding what goes into the context window on every call: instructions, files, history, tool results. Most agent failures start here.
items.title: Context engineering explained: What every AI developer should know
items.why: Defines the term in the first minute, names four ways a long context goes wrong, and shows the four fixes on one small agent.

items.what: When the window fills up, summarise the old part, keep the decisions, drop the chatter, and carry on.
items.title: Context Management in Claude Code
items.why: Three minutes from the team that built it: what compaction keeps, what it can lose, and what to put in a file instead. One line is out of date: MCP tools no longer all load into context by default.

items.what: Checks before and after the model: block the bad request, catch the bad answer, before a user sees it.
items.title: What are AI guardrails? How do they work?
items.why: A security and privacy practitioner sorts the word into its real types, and is honest that every one of them can be got around.

items.what: Text hidden in an email, a web page or a file that tells your model to do something else. The attack every agent with tools has to plan for.
items.title: Prompt Injection, Clearly Explained
items.why: Why a model cannot tell instructions from data, one email attack walked through, and defences you can use in your own app.

items.what: Tests for AI output. A fixed set of cases you run after every change, so you know if it got better or worse.
items.title: The Most Important Skill for AI Engineers: Evals Explained
items.why: Written for people building products: why public benchmarks do not test your app, and a first eval built end to end.

items.what: A second model grades the answers against a rubric, when there is no single right answer to compare with.
items.title: LLM-as-a-judge: evaluating LLMs with LLMs
items.why: Under six minutes on building a judge you can trust: label some answers yourself first, and check the judge agrees with you.

items.what: A record of every step an agent took: each prompt, tool call and result. How you find the step that broke.
items.title: LLM Observability Explained: Why Your AI Lies to You
items.why: Not tied to any product. A trace is the full story of one request, and each step in it is a span.

items.what: Send easy requests to a small, cheap model and hard ones to a big one. Same quality, a smaller bill.
items.title: What is an LLM Router?
items.why: Clear on the idea in two minutes. From 2024, so the model names are old, and its “over 85% savings” holds for one benchmark only. The idea has not changed.

blocks.title: How these videos were picked
blocks.html: For each term we shortlisted three or four videos: from YouTube search, and by searching Reddit, Hacker News and practitioners' blogs for what developers recommend. Then we read the full transcript of every shortlisted video (about 50 in all) and checked it for four things: is it correct and still current, is it clear for someone new to the term, is it about the term and not a sales pitch, and is it worth the time. Several popular videos were dropped for real mistakes, like saying one technique stops a model from making things up. Where we found a flaw that matters in a pick, the line under it says so. No video here is sponsored, and nobody paid to be on the list. Checked 5 to 6 November 2026. If you find a better video for any term, tell us on Instagram.
